parsed.explanation: The combined regime layers a hostile national framework onto a division with the country's broadest bathroom criminalisation. Traveller-facing exposures are documented and universal: binary sex-marker passports (X processing halted), visa officers instructed to refuse cases with document/sex discrepancies and to consider lifetime fraud findings, allied governments issuing trans-specific travel advisories, and nationwide facility bans in many units. The division adds its own hostile layer — a 2026 statute criminalising restroom use in private businesses and government buildings, up to a year in jail — so it cannot sit above the parent average. National custody harms (forced labour, sexual abuse, conversion-style policies) and state threat-framing ('radical gender ideology') are documented. Mitigations: pending constitutional suit, no documented enforcement against visitors, no documented trans-specific violence above background, partial hate-crime and anti-discrimination machinery. Severe exposure, imperfect remedies, but not tier-0 lethality.

entry_documents.exposure: National passports reissued as binary birth sex; X markers halted; travellers report confiscated passports and stranding; visa cable directs refusal on sex-document discrepancy and possible lifetime fraud ineligibility; foreign governments advise caution.
entry_documents.protection: Passport restrictions enjoined-then-allowed by Supreme Court remain in litigation; existing X passports valid until expiry; legal-aid FAQ exists.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry screening drives outing at the border; a state-issued credential may diverge from passport marker, compounding checks.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Documented national custody harms: conversion-style policies for trans inmates, hormone removal, immigration-custody forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse; reporting on trans prisoner numbers ended.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: None documented for foreign detainees; several national orders enjoined in court.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A restroom statute arrest or visa fraud finding can route a visitor into national custody with these documented conditions.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law (effective 1 July 2026) criminalises restroom/changing use by birth sex in government buildings AND private businesses — hospitals, restaurants, gas stations; up to 1 year jail first offence. Facility bans documented across many units.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Constitutional suit filed 30 April 2026; exemption carve-outs (chaperoning, emergencies) narrow the offence; 40% of the division population covered by local protections.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State statute is the operative rule for daily facility access; national government-building bans overlap.

care_services.exposure: Hospitals are covered by the division bathroom law; national subpoenas of hospital records for minors; care for minors banned in 27 units; visitor care access uncertainty.
care_services.protection: Division prisoners may receive hormone therapy per 2024 national ruling; 22 units outlaw gender-identity discrimination.
care_services.interaction: Seeking care or travelling with a minor exposes records and identity to institutions.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: State framing of trans people as risk: binary-sex executive orders, 'gender ideology' removals, counterterrorism strategy targeting 'radically pro-transgender' groups; bathroom law treats entry as criminal trespass.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Several orders enjoined; national employment-discrimination ruling and hate-crime statute remain in force.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official hostility raises outing probability and shapes enforcement discretion nationwide.

minors_guardians.exposure: Teachers/clinicians must disclose a minor's trans status to parents within 3 days; criminal prosecution threatened for staff facilitating social transition; hospitals subpoenaed; a prior bill proposed life imprisonment for parents seeking out-of-unit care.
minors_guardians.protection: Bill blocked in upper chamber; suits pending.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling parent with a trans minor faces forced outing and potential investigation.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: One documented arrest under a unit bathroom law (student handcuffed, 24h men's-ward detention); no state-specific data showing trans violence above general homicide rate.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime statute nationally; partial state coverage; civil-rights litigation functioning.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Police may enforce restroom statutes; response to violence varies by unit.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Enforcement of the division law against visitors not documented but the universal exposure persists; felony/misdemeanour classification unresolved; litigation outcomes open.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active constitutional litigation; legal-aid resources; some units protective (sanctuary-like scorecards).
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Travel exposure depends on measures in force at time of travel; uncertainty cuts both ways.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A's exclusion register denies entry and humiliates universally with no remedy. This jurisdiction's universal exposures (document regime, bathroom criminalisation reaching private businesses) are comparable in breadth, but consequences documented here are misdemeanour-level arrest and hostile custody rather than systematic entry denial — slightly above, but the division's own hostile layer keeps it near this anchor.

0.55-B's worst feature is secondary screening and refused admission — administrative, humiliating, with functioning appeal desks. This jurisdiction is materially worse: criminal statute, custody harms, and lifetime fraud findings are documented, so it sits below 0.55-B.

0.75-C has trained officers, tribunal remedies, and brief detentions. Here remedies are partial and contested, the state itself is the threat-framing actor, and the division criminalises daily facility use — far below this anchor.

0.25-E's shelters exclude by birth sex with assault routine and no remedy. This jurisdiction has documented custody abuse but also functioning litigation, hate-crime law, and no trans-specific violence above background — above 0.25-E but not comfortably.

0.45-A's registry-driven everyday exposure with inconsistent enforcement closely parallels this case's document/facility regime. The division's broader criminalisation and documented custody abuse push this rating to the bottom of that band.

0.15-C's organised sweeps, coerced confessions, and failed recourse are absent here: no documented visitor sweeps, courts are actively litigating, and no lethal pathway is established — well above this anchor.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime the traveller meets is the union of national and division rules. The national layer supplies universal document exposure: binary passports, refusal instructions at visa adjudication, and foreign-government advisories confirming that other states treat this as a real risk. The division layer adds the harshest documented facility rule — criminalisation reaching private businesses with up to a year's imprisonment — making the traveller's everyday exposure (every restroom visit, every hospital entry) legally hazardous, and because the division adds its own hostile layer it cannot score above the parent's average. Custody harms and counterterrorism threat-framing mean that if the chain document-check → investigation → detention fires, conditions are documented as abusive. Mitigations are real but partial: active constitutional litigation, functioning courts, partial hate-crime coverage, no documented visitor enforcement, and no trans-specific violence above background. The result is severe, universal, state-imposed exposure with thin but nonzero recourse — High Risk, near the top of the band, ~0.38.
